summary: This RFC is the official specification of the format of the Internet host table, the file listing host names and addresses. It brings RFC 810 up to date with minor revisions.

plainLanguage.summary: Before the Domain Name System, name and address information lived in one central file called HOSTS.TXT. This memo is the official description of that file: the rules for choosing names, the four kinds of entry, and the exact six-field format of a line. Every machine copied the file and translated it into whatever form it needed.

questions: what was the internet host table format
what characters are allowed in a host name
what does a hosts.txt entry look like
subtitle: The official format of HOSTS.TXT, the single file that listed every host name, address and service on the early Internet.

tldr.problem: In the early Internet, every host needed a name and a 32-bit address, and there had to be one authoritative, machine-readable list that everyone could translate into their own format.
tldr.mechanism: The DoD Internet Host Table is a plain ASCII file of NET, GATEWAY, HOST and DOMAIN entries, each a fixed six-field line, distributed from the SRI-NIC host by FTP or the NIC hostname server.
tldr.outcome: It is an old specification: the RFC obsoletes RFC 810 (and RFC 608) and was itself updated by RFC 1123, and the host table approach was later displaced by the Domain Name System.

today: RFC 952 is an old specification, published in October 1985, that obsoletes RFC 810 and RFC 608 and has been updated by RFC 1123. The unit metadata records its status as unknown, reflecting its age; the central host table it defines was superseded by the Domain Name System.

sections.title: The Internet Host Table
sections.content:
This RFC is the official specification of the format of the Internet Host Table. This edition includes minor revisions to RFC 810 that bring it up to date, and it also obsoletes RFC 608. The DoD Host Table is used by the DoD Hostname Server, which is maintained by the DDN Network Information Center on behalf of the Defense Communications Agency.

A machine-translatable ASCII version of the table is kept online in the file NETINFO:HOSTS.TXT on the SRI-NIC host. It can be fetched by FTP by connecting to SRI-NIC.ARPA, logging in as the anonymous user, and retrieving the file, or it can be obtained through the NIC Hostname Server; the latter is faster and easier but needs a program to make the connection. It is the responsibility of the users of the table to translate it into whatever format they need.
sections.plainLanguage: One central machine kept the master list of names and addresses, and everyone else copied it. The file was plain text so that any computer could convert it into its own local form, and it could be picked up either by file transfer or by asking the name server.

sections.title: Names and Addresses
sections.content:
A name, whether a Net, Host, Gateway or Domain name, is a text string of up to 24 characters drawn from the letters A to Z, the digits 0 to 9, the minus sign and the period. Periods are allowed only where they delimit the components of domain-style names. No spaces or blanks are allowed, upper and lower case are not distinguished, the first character must be a letter, and the last character must not be a minus sign or a period. Single-character names and nicknames are not allowed.

Special conventions apply to certain roles. A host that serves as a gateway should have "-GATEWAY" or "-GW" as part of its name, and hosts that are not gateways should not use those strings. A host that is a TAC should have "-TAC" as the last part of its name if it is a DoD host. Internet addresses are 32-bit, written in the table as four decimal numbers separated by periods, each representing one octet.

The first bits of the address determine its class. If the first bit is 0, the next 7 bits give a Class A network number. If the first two bits are 1 and 0, the next 14 bits give a Class B network number. If the first three bits are 1, 1 and 0, the next 21 bits give a Class C network number. The remaining bits form the local address of the host within that network.
sections.plainLanguage: Names were short, made only of letters, digits, dots and dashes, and could not start with a digit or end with a dot or a dash. A name's ending told you a host's job, such as a gateway. Addresses were written as four numbers, and the way the first bits of the first number began told you how the network part and the host part were divided.

sections.title: Entry Format
sections.content:
Each host table entry is an ASCII text string of six fields. Field 1 is the keyword saying whether the entry is a NET, GATEWAY, HOST or DOMAIN. Field 2 is the Internet address, followed by any alternate addresses. Field 3 is the official name, with optional nicknames where they are permitted. Fields 4, 5 and 6 are the machine type, the operating system and the protocol list, and they are optional; for a domain they are not used. Fields 3 to 6, if present, describe the first address in field 2.

A colon is the field delimiter and a comma is the data element delimiter; two colons together mark a null field, and a semicolon begins a comment that runs to the end of the line. Blanks are ignored between data elements or fields but are not allowed inside a data element, and each entry ends with a colon. A protocol item may be written as TRANSPORT/SERVICE, as a transport alone, or as a service alone. Continuation lines begin with at least one blank and may be used wherever blanks are legal.

NET entries are assigned and cannot have alternate addresses or nicknames, and nicknames are not permitted for NET names. DOMAIN entries use only the first three fields. Optional nicknames are allowed for hosts but are discouraged, except when a host name has changed and both the new and the old names are kept for a time to smooth the transition. Entries are grouped by type in the order Domain, Net, Gateway and Host, and within a type the ordering is unspecified.
sections.plainLanguage: Every line is a fixed pattern of six parts separated by colons: what the entry is, its address, its official name, and then optional machine, software and service details. Punctuation has strict jobs, comments start with a semicolon, and the file is grouped by entry type.

sections.title: An Example Table
sections.content:
The RFC gives a short example that shows all the entry kinds in use. A network entry looks like NET : 10.0.0.0 : ARPANET :. A gateway entry gives two addresses and two names, followed by its machine type, operating system and protocols: GATEWAY : 10.0.0.77, 18.10.0.4 : MIT-GW.ARPA,MIT-GATEWAY : PDP-11 : MOS : IP/GW,EGP :. A host entry can list alternate addresses and several transport and service pairs: HOST : 26.0.0.73, 10.0.0.51 : SRI-NIC.ARPA,SRI-NIC,NIC : DEC-2060 : TOPS20 : TCP/TELNET,TCP/SMTP,TCP/TIME,TCP/FTP,TCP/ECHO,ICMP :.

The protocol list uses the TRANSPORT/SERVICE form, where both parts may be given as in TCP/TELNET, only the transport as in a bare transport name, or only the service. The RFC refers the reader to the assigned numbers for the specific options and acronyms for machine types, operating systems and protocol and service names.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show how real entries look, including a host with two addresses and a list of the services it offers, written as a transport and a service joined by a slash.

sections.title: Registration and What Came Next
sections.content:
Names and addresses for DoD hosts and gateways were negotiated and registered with the DDN PMO and then with the NIC before being used and before traffic was passed by a DoD host. Names and addresses for domains and networks were registered with the DDN Network Information Center. The NIC would also keep similar information for non-DoD networks and hosts if it was provided, and for as long as it was needed, that is until intercommunicating network name servers were in place.

That final qualification points to the host table's fate. The table was a single central file that every host had to copy and keep current, which does not scale, and the RFC's own references look forward to the Domain Name System and its implementation schedule. This document obsoletes RFC 810 and RFC 608 and was itself updated by RFC 1123.
sections.plainLanguage: Names had to be registered centrally before they could be used, and the file was only meant to last until a proper distributed name service existed. That service, the Domain Name System, replaced the single-file approach because one central file could not keep up with a growing Internet.
